title: Search a 2D Matrix II
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every cell versus a staircase two-pointer walk from the top-right corner exploiting the doubly-sorted structure.

blocks.text: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for a value target in an m x n integer matrix, where every row is sorted in ascending order (left to right), and every column is sorted in ascending order (top to bottom). Return true if target exists in the matrix, false otherwise.

blocks.caption: Walk a staircase path from the top-right corner, eliminating a row or column at each step

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An m x n integer matrix, ascending along every row and every column, and an integer target"],["Output","true if target exists anywhere in the matrix, false otherwise"],["Goal","Search efficiently, exploiting the doubly-sorted structure rather than checking every cell"],["Constraints","m == matrix.length; n == matrix[i].length; 1 <= m, n <= 300; -10^9 <= matrix[i][j] <= 10^9; -10^9 <= target <= 10^9"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The matrix is sorted in BOTH row and column directions simultaneously","A staircase-style two-pointer walk that eliminates an entire row or column at each step, the same family of technique as Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix"],["Starting from a corner where one direction increases and the other also increases","The top-right (or bottom-left) corner is the ideal starting point, since moving in either direction gives a clean, predictable value change"],["A single comparison at each step definitively rules out an entire row or column","No need for backtracking; every step makes irreversible, guaranteed progress toward the target or its absence"]]}

blocks.text: Given a matrix sorted in ascending order along both rows and columns, determine whether a given target value exists anywhere in it.

blocks.title: Analogy: Navigating a City Grid Where Addresses Increase Both East and South
blocks.text: Like searching for a specific address in a city grid where street numbers increase both heading east and heading south. Starting from the northeast corner (the highest-numbered street heading east, lowest heading south), if the current address is too high, moving west (west addresses are lower) makes sense; if too low, moving south (south addresses are higher) makes sense. Either way, one entire direction of unnecessary searching is eliminated with each single comparison.

blocks.caption: Too big means move left, eliminating a column; too small means move down, eliminating a row

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Starting at top-right (0,4)=15: too big, move left; (0,3)=11: too big, move left; (0,2)=7: too big, move left; (0,1)=4: too small, move down; (1,1)=5: match!","Found at (1,1)","Each comparison correctly eliminates an entire row or column of candidates"],["Answer","true","target 5 exists in the matrix"]]}

blocks.text: Example: matrix = same as above, target = 20

blocks.text: Before checking every single cell, notice that starting from the right corner, a single comparison can definitively rule out an entire row or column at once, thanks to the matrix being sorted in two directions.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Starting at the top-right corner, moving LEFT along a row only ever decreases values, and moving DOWN along a column only ever increases values.

Observation 2: If the current cell's value is greater than target, then every cell BELOW it in the same column is even larger (column is ascending top to bottom), so none of them can possibly equal target either; it's safe to move left, abandoning this entire column.

Observation 3: If the current cell's value is less than target, then every cell to its LEFT in the same row is even smaller (row is ascending left to right), so none of them can possibly equal target either; it's safe to move down, abandoning this entire row.

Observation 4: This process continues until either target is found (a match), or the pointers walk off the matrix entirely (target doesn't exist).

Recognizing that a single comparison, from the right starting corner, can always rule out an entire row OR column definitively (never both are ambiguous at once) is what makes this staircase technique correct and efficient.

This is the classic staircase two-pointer search, the same family of technique used in Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix, adapted here for finding a specific target rather than counting negatives.
Check every single cell in the matrix directly, comparing it against target.

items: Iterate over every row and every column of the matrix.
For every cell, check whether it equals target, returning true immediately if a match is found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every cell is visited using a straightforward nested loop, since this brute force does not yet exploit the sorted structure at all.
The function returns true immediately upon finding a match, avoiding unnecessary further checking.
If the loops complete without any match, false is correctly returned.

blocks.text: Every cell is checked directly, so the correct true/false result is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m * n), potentially visiting every cell.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: checking every cell individually ignores that the matrix being sorted along BOTH rows and columns guarantees an entire row or column can be eliminated from consideration with just a single comparison.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every cell. Instead, start at the top-right corner and use two pointers (row, col). At each step, compare the current cell to target: if it matches, return true immediately; if it's too big, move left (eliminating the current column, since everything below is even bigger); if it's too small, move down (eliminating the current row, since everything to the left is even smaller). This walk visits at most m + n cells total.

Start with row = 0 and col = n - 1. While both pointers remain in bounds: if matrix[row][col] equals target, return true; if it's greater than target, decrement col; otherwise, increment row. Return false if the pointers exit the matrix without finding a match.
Walk a staircase path from the top-right corner, eliminating an entire row or column at each step.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The target 5 is found at (1,1), matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), since row only ever increases and col only ever decreases, together moving at most m + n times total.
Space: O(1) extra.

Starting at the top-right corner, moving left always decreases value (row is ascending left to right) and moving down always increases value (column is ascending top to bottom). This means from any current position, a value greater than target guarantees every cell below the current one in this column is also greater (safe to eliminate the whole column by moving left), and a value less than target guarantees every cell to the left in this row is also smaller (safe to eliminate the whole row by moving down). Every comparison therefore makes guaranteed, irreversible progress.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["matrix[row][col] == target","Target found; return true immediately"],["matrix[row][col] > target","Move left, eliminating the current column (everything below is even bigger)"],["matrix[row][col] < target","Move down, eliminating the current row (everything to the left is even smaller)"]]}

items: Starting at the TOP-RIGHT corner (not top-left or any other corner) is essential, since it's the only corner where moving in each of the two directions produces a clean, single-direction value change.
row only ever increases and col only ever decreases, so the total number of steps is bounded by m + n, never more.
The loop condition (row < rows && col >= 0) correctly terminates the search once either pointer exits the matrix.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (check every cell)","O(m * n)","O(1) extra","Every cell is individually checked, ignoring the sorted structure entirely"],["Optimized (staircase walk from top-right)","O(m + n)","O(1) extra","Exploits the doubly-sorted structure to eliminate an entire row or column per step"]]}

blocks.text: When a grid is sorted along both axes simultaneously, a single "staircase" pointer walk from the appropriate corner can eliminate entire rows or columns per step, turning an O(m*n) full scan into an O(m+n) search, the same underlying idea as Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix.

items: Starting from the wrong corner (e.g., top-left), where BOTH directions increase, making it impossible to cleanly eliminate a row or column with a single comparison.

Confusing this problem with the simpler "Search a 2D Matrix I" (where each row's last element is less than the next row's first, allowing a single binary search over the whole matrix treated as one sorted array); this problem's weaker sorting guarantee requires the staircase technique instead.
Moving in the wrong direction after a comparison (e.g., moving down instead of left when the value is too big), which would fail to correctly eliminate the intended row or column.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["target is smaller than every element, or larger than every element","The staircase walk correctly exits the matrix bounds without finding a match, returning false"],["matrix has only 1 row or 1 column","The staircase walk degenerates naturally to a simple linear scan along that single row or column"],["target appears multiple times in the matrix","The walk returns true the moment it encounters any one occurrence, without needing to find every occurrence"]]}

items: Explicitly justify why the top-right (or equivalently, bottom-left) corner is the only valid starting point for this staircase technique, since interviewers often specifically probe why the top-left corner would NOT work here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Matrix sorted along BOTH rows and columns (but NOT necessarily as one single fully sorted sequence), search for a target" points toward a staircase two-pointer walk from the top-right (or bottom-left) corner, eliminating an entire row or column per step.

items: How does this differ from "Search a 2D Matrix I"? That problem's stronger guarantee (each row's last element is less than the next row's first) means the whole matrix can be treated as one single sorted sequence, searchable via standard binary search in O(log(m*n)); this problem's weaker guarantee requires the O(m+n) staircase technique instead.

How would you find the COUNT of occurrences of target, not just whether it exists? The staircase technique alone doesn't directly give a count; a different approach (e.g., counting elements less than or equal to target using a similar staircase idea) would be needed.

Could this be solved with binary search on each row independently? Yes, giving O(m log n) time, slower than the O(m+n) staircase for large, roughly square matrices, but sometimes simpler to reason about.
The same staircase two-pointer technique used in Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix elsewhere in this category, here adapted for target search instead of counting negatives.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m * n) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (staircase walk): O(m + n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Staircase two-pointer walk from the top-right corner, exploiting a doubly-sorted matrix
Core Idea: A value too big eliminates the current column (move left); a value too small eliminates the current row (move down)
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Starting at the top-right corner, every single comparison definitively rules out an entire row or column, since moving left only decreases and moving down only increases
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: From the top-right, too big means go left, too small means go down
